A system for asking plainly, and showing what came back.

Payday is the design system behind FairShift. Warm paper, serif headlines and flat white cards on the page, with product shots and photographs of people at work side by side. Every component here is shadcn/ui, restyled from one DESIGN.md.

Icons

Hugeicons, in a hairline stroke, at the size the component sets. Use them for actions, never as bullets.

Actions

Things people press. Blue means act here, so each view gets one blue button and everything beside it is quieter.

Button

Starts an action. A pill, 44px tall, 48px for marketing calls to action.

Button group

Joins actions that belong to one thing, such as an export and its formats, or stepping between pay periods.

Toggle

Turns one view option on or off and keeps showing which it is. For a setting that saves, use a switch.

Toggle group

Picks from two to seven options that are all visible at once. One choice by default, several with multiple.

Badge

Labels the status of a row: an open flag, a fix, a count. A tag with 4px corners, never a pill and never a button.

Kbd

Shows a keyboard shortcut next to the action it runs. Set in the same sans as everything else.

Inputs

How an owner sets up a check-in and how the team answers it. Every control is 44px tall and fully rounded, and the label always says what to enter.

Field

Wraps every control with its label, help text and error. Forms are a field group of fields, never loose inputs.

Input

One line of text: a name, a number, an email. Use a field around it so it always has a label.

Input group

An input with something attached: an icon, a prefix, a unit, or a button that acts on what was typed.

Textarea

More than one line: the question you send, or a note in the fix log. It grows with what is typed.

Select

One choice from a short, known list, such as a pay schedule. If the list is long enough to search, use a combobox.

Native select

The browser's own select. Use it where the phone's built-in picker is the better experience, or where the page must work before scripts load.

Combobox

A select you can type into. Use it when the list is long, or when people know the name they are looking for.

Checkbox

Any number of choices from a list, or one thing to agree to. It takes effect when the form is saved.

Radio group

Exactly one choice from a few options that are worth reading side by side. This is also how an employee answers.

Switch

A setting that is on or off and takes effect straight away. If it waits for a save button, use a checkbox.

Slider

A number where the rough position matters more than the exact figure. Always show the value next to it.

Input OTP

A short code we texted to someone. One box per digit, so it is obvious how many are left.

Calendar

Picks a day or a run of days when seeing the week matters: the next payday, or the pay period a fix log covers.

Label

The name of a control. Inside a form, use the field label; this is the bare label for a control that stands alone.

Right to left

The same components inside a direction provider. Labels, icons and menus mirror; nothing is rebuilt.

Navigation

How an owner moves through the app: between views of one pay period, back up to the report, and across the fix log.

Tabs

Switch between views of the same thing, such as one pay period. Not for moving between pages.

Breadcrumb

Show where a page sits and give a way back up. Use it from the second level down.

Pagination

Page through a long list that has a known length, such as the fix log.

Navigation menu

Top-level site navigation where a section needs a short panel of links. Open Report or Roster to see one.

Menubar

A row of menus for a dense working view, such as the report toolbar. Rare in this product.

Sidebar

The app's main navigation. Five places, in the order an owner uses them on payday.

Data display

How the product shows what happened on payday: who replied, what they flagged, and what was done about it.

Card

An inset panel that groups one subject. A filled panel with no border, set straight on the page.

Table

Records with the same fields, read across and compared down. The fix log and the roster are tables.

Chart

A trend or a comparison the owner should see at a glance. Blue is the series that matters, ink and greys carry the rest.

Item

One thing in a list with a title, a line of detail and an action. Lighter than a card, richer than a table row.

Avatar

A person on the roster or an admin. Initials stand in whenever there is no photo, which is most of the time.

Accordion

A set of questions or rows where reading one at a time is enough. One opens, the others close.

Collapsible

One section that can be tucked away, such as flags that are already fixed.

Carousel

A few panels of the same kind where one at a time is enough, such as a location each.

Scroll area

A list that is longer than the space it has, inside a panel that should not grow.

Resizable

Two panes the owner may want to rebalance, such as a list of flags beside the one being read. Drag the hairline.

Aspect ratio

Hold a shape for a photograph or a preview before it loads, so the page does not jump.

Separator

A hairline between things that belong together. The system divides with lines and space, not boxes.

Code block

Something to copy exactly: a webhook payload, an export command, an import error. Set in the same sans, with tabular figures.

Feedback

How the product tells an owner what happened. A flag is a plain sentence with a next step, and nothing counts as done until the fix is logged.

Alert

A message that stays on the page until it stops being true. Use the destructive variant only for something urgent or broken.

Toast

A short confirmation of something the owner just did. It leaves on its own, so never use it for anything they must read.

Progress

How far along something measurable is: answers in, rows imported. For work with no known length, use a spinner.

Spinner

Something is happening and we cannot say how long it will take. Put it inside the control that started the work.

Skeleton

A placeholder in the shape of what is loading, so the page does not jump when the content arrives.

Empty

A list with nothing in it yet. Say why it is empty and, if there is one, give the single next thing to do.

Overlays

Layers that sit above the page. They are the only surfaces in the system that take a shadow. Each one opens from a button that says what it opens.

Dialog

A short task that needs an answer before the owner carries on, such as logging a fix.

Alert dialog

A confirmation before something that cannot be undone from the same screen. Name the consequence, and label the button with the action.

Sheet

Detail about one thing in a list, opened from the side so the list stays in view behind it.

Drawer

A bottom panel for a short step on a phone. It can be swiped away.

Popover

A small set of choices attached to the button that opened it. It does not block the page.

Hover card

A preview of something a link points to. Nothing inside it should be the only way to reach anything.

Tooltip

The name of a control that has no visible label, or one short line about what a button will do.

Dropdown menu

The actions for one thing, behind one button. Put the destructive action last, on its own.

Context menu

The same actions on right-click or press and hold. Only ever a shortcut, never the only way.

Command

Search across flags, people and actions from the keyboard. Shown inline here; in the product it opens in a dialog.

Conversation

The product is a text message, so the thread is the most important screen there is. FairShift speaks in a frosted tint. The employee always answers in blue.

Message scroller

Any thread that scrolls. It keeps its own scroll position, follows new texts and offers a way back to the latest one.

Message

One row of a thread: who said it, what they said and when. The employee's side is the end; everyone else is the start.

Bubble

The surface a text sits on. Pick the variant by who is speaking, not by how it looks.

Attachment

A file or a voice note in a thread or a form. It carries its own upload state, so there is no separate spinner.

Marker

A line in a thread that nobody said: a date, a system note, the moment a fix was logged.

Trace

What FairShift did with a reply, one line per step. A line opens only when there is something behind it.

Questionnaire

The same check-in on a screen instead of by text: one question at a time, each one optional.

Do and don't

Five rules that are easy to break, shown both ways.

One blue thing

One primary action per view. A second action is ink or quiet.

Pills, not boxes

Buttons, fields and tags are fully rounded. Cards and panels take the large soft corner.

Flat cards

A card is white on paper. It takes no border and no drop shadow.

Dots, not ticks

A list of points takes a small blue dot. Ticks are kept out of lists.

Sentence case, no eyebrows

A serif heading stands on its own. Size carries emphasis, not capitals or bold.

Recipes

The pieces the FairShift site is made of, rebuilt from the components and tokens above.

Hero

A dark rounded panel set in from the page edges. Serif headline on the left; on the right a photograph with the check-in playing over it.

Ask every employee, every payday.

FairShift texts your hourly team three quick questions each pay period.

Did you get all your meal and rest breaks this pay period?
No. I worked a double on Saturday.

Feature card

A product shot on a paper inset, then a serif title and two lines of text. Cards sit 0.75rem apart in a grid.

roster.csvNameMobileLanguageLocation

Zero setup

Upload a roster and pick the pay schedule. Questions, languages and timing come preset.

Built for the people on the line, and read in under a minute.

Person and product

A photograph of the person being asked, with their reply in blue and the card it becomes on the report. People and product share the frame.

Did you get all your meal and rest breaks this pay period?

No. I worked a double on Saturday.

Missed meal break

Pay one hour of premium pay and check Saturday for back-to-back doubles.

Status tags

Green means a fix is logged, amber means a flag is open, red means urgent. Nothing else is coloured.

Panel

The paper-2 surface, 1.5rem corners. It groups white cards; a white card never sits directly inside another.

Fewer surprises, and less time on people problems.

No dashboard to learn. You read one page each pay period and mark issues fixed.

  • A report you can read in a minute
  • A clear next step for every flag
  • Alerts that skip the manager they name
